scenarios.requirement: Unauthenticated IRC clients cannot send channel messages.
Unauthenticated IRC clients cannot send DMs.
Unauthenticated clients cannot JOIN channels.
NICK and USER alone do not authenticate a session.
Valid account credentials authenticate successfully.
Invalid passwords are rejected.
Unknown accounts are rejected.
Disabled accounts cannot authenticate.
Deleted accounts cannot authenticate.
Expired sessions cannot access REST APIs.
Revoked sessions cannot access REST APIs.
Incorrect credentials never create a usable session.
Successful login resolves the correct stable account identity.
NickServ and REST authentication resolve the same account.
SASL authentication resolves the same account.
Authentication restores legitimate account-based ChanServ permissions.
Authentication does not automatically confer channel privileges the account doesn't possess.
Ordinary account creation cannot assign administrator privileges.
User-controlled registration properties cannot inject privileged roles.
Account signup restrictions are enforced.
Multiple failed logins trigger appropriate rate limits.
Logging out invalidates the relevant session.
Password reset invalidates sessions according to the defined security policy.
Account disable revokes active access.
Reenabling an account does not silently reactivate previously revoked sessions.
Authentication credentials do not appear in public API responses or logs.
Malformed SASL and SCRAM exchanges fail safely.
SCRAM authentication matches published cryptographic test vectors.
Unknown users and invalid passwords do not expose unnecessary account-enumeration information.
Pre-authentication IRC commands are limited to the permitted authentication and registration flow.
Administrator can list accounts.
Administrator can inspect permitted account administration metadata.
Administrator can disable an account.
Administrator can reenable an account.
Administrator can revoke a session.
Administrator can disconnect an active IRC user.
Administrator can assign network roles within their authority.
Administrator can remove network roles.
Administrator can register a channel administratively.
Administrator can inspect channel configuration.
Administrator can change network-controlled channel settings.
Administrator can apply global bans.
Administrator can remove global bans.
Administrator can broadcast network notices.
Administrator can inspect operational statistics.
Administrator can inspect appropriate administrative audit logs.
Administrator can manage service-bot configuration.
Administrator can revoke compromised bot credentials.
Ordinary users cannot enumerate all accounts through admin APIs.
Ordinary users cannot disable other accounts.
Ordinary users cannot reset other users' passwords.
Ordinary users cannot assign network-wide roles.
Ordinary users cannot revoke other users' sessions.
Ordinary users cannot issue network-wide announcements.
Channel founders cannot impersonate network administrators.
IRC operators cannot perform network-administrator-only actions unless explicitly delegated.
Administrators cannot exceed their configured privilege scope.
No administrator API can be accessed through an unprotected legacy alias.
Administrative requests are audited with actor, action, target and outcome.
Rejected administrative attempts do not modify state.
Alice can view her own profile.
Alice can update permitted fields on her own profile.
Alice cannot modify Bob's profile.
Alice cannot change Bob's avatar.
Alice cannot change Bob's display name.
Alice cannot change Bob's status.
Alice cannot change Bob's password.
Alice cannot change Bob's email or recovery credentials, if supported.
Alice cannot retrieve Bob's password hashes or SCRAM credential material.
Alice cannot add herself to another user's registered nicknames.
Alice cannot remove Bob's registered nickname.
Alice cannot set her own `isAdmin` or equivalent field.
Alice cannot assign herself a privileged account role.
Mass-assignment attempts using additional JSON properties are rejected or safely ignored.
Public profile endpoints do not expose private account metadata.
Profile updates propagate correctly to subscribed IRC clients.
Profile updates propagate correctly to authorized REST/event clients.
Private profile metadata is excluded from public metadata synchronization.
Disabled accounts cannot update profiles using existing sessions.
Account deletion follows the documented data-retention policy without deleting unrelated data.
Authenticated users can join ordinary public channels.
Joined users can send messages when permitted.
Users can leave a channel.
Leaving removes active membership.
Users cannot impersonate another member when joining.
Membership is restored or reconciled correctly after reconnects according to policy.
Unauthorized users cannot discover secret channels through LIST.
Unauthorized users cannot discover secret channels through REST discovery.
Unauthorized users cannot enumerate secret-channel members.
Unauthorized users cannot retrieve secret-channel history.
Unauthorized users cannot subscribe to secret-channel events.
Unauthorized users cannot retrieve secret-channel attachment metadata.
Authorized members can access permitted secret-channel resources.
Revoked members lose future access.
History access before joining and after leaving follows an explicit documented policy.
Uninvited users cannot join invite-only channels.
Invitations grant only the intended access.
Invitations cannot be forged by ordinary members.
Revoked invitations cannot be reused.
Incorrect channel keys are rejected.
Channel keys are not exposed through unauthorized APIs or events.
REST and IRC enforce identical JOIN policies.
API-created membership cannot bypass invite/key restrictions.
Expired or consumed invitations cannot be replayed when applicable.
Banned users cannot rejoin.
Banned users cannot bypass restrictions using REST.
Banned users cannot publish messages through the API.
Banned users cannot receive restricted real-time events.
Ban exceptions work only when their defined conditions match.
Bans remain effective after disconnect/reconnect.
Nickname changes do not bypass account-based restrictions.
Membership data does not remain incorrectly authorized after a KICK.
Channel removal and re-registration do not accidentally retain stale permissions.
Founder can manage channel settings.
Founder can create permitted role groups.
Founder can assign roles within the policy.
Founder can remove roles.
Founder can configure the F service bot.
Founder can transfer ownership only through the authorized ownership-transfer flow.
Another user cannot impersonate the founder.
Channel administrators can perform their explicitly assigned moderation actions.
Channel administrators cannot assign privileges above their own.
Channel administrators cannot take ownership without authorization.
Operators can kick users when permitted.
Operators can ban users when permitted.
Operators can change permitted channel modes.
Operators cannot perform founder-only actions.
Half-operators cannot modify higher-ranked users when prohibited by the configured hierarchy.
Half-operators cannot assign operator privileges unless explicitly authorized.
Operators in `#public` have no automatic privileges in `#staff`.
Voiced users can speak in moderated channels.
Ordinary users cannot speak in moderated channels unless independently permitted.
Voiced users cannot kick or ban members.
Ordinary users cannot change channel modes.
Ordinary users cannot change channel roles.
Ordinary users cannot modify restricted channel metadata.
Ordinary users cannot assign themselves voice through the REST API.
Custom role names do not automatically grant privileges.
Custom permissions are applied consistently.
Removing a role immediately removes its associated permissions.
Custom permissions cannot escalate beyond the assigning actor's authority.
Deleting a role removes or safely reconciles assignments.
Role assignments survive restarts.
Role changes update IRC prefix modes where applicable.
IRC mode changes update API-visible role state where applicable.
Role changes invalidate cached permissions.
Role inheritance cannot create privilege-escalation cycles.
A malicious user cannot grant themselves access by creating a similarly named role.
Cross-channel role IDs cannot be reused to modify unrelated channels.
Alice can send messages to a public channel she is authorized to use.
Alice cannot send into a restricted channel she cannot access.
Alice cannot forge Bob's sender identity.
Alice cannot forge a server/service prefix.
Alice cannot forge privileged server-generated account or role tags.
Alice can edit her own message when editing is permitted.
Alice cannot edit Bob's message.
Alice cannot edit messages in inaccessible channels.
Alice cannot use another channel's message ID to edit a different message.
Editing produces correct persistent state.
Editing produces correct authorized real-time events.
Editing survives object reactivation.
Unauthorized edits produce no data changes or events.
Alice can redact her own message when policy permits.
Alice cannot redact Bob's message without moderation privileges.
Authorized moderators can redact messages according to policy.
Moderation does not silently rewrite a message as though its author edited it.
Redacted messages do not reappear through CHATHISTORY.
Redacted messages do not reappear through REST history.
Reply references cannot expose restricted messages.
Reactions, if supported, respect channel access.
Editing or deleting nonexistent messages produces a safe error.
Duplicate message IDs cannot overwrite unrelated messages.
Message ordering and sequence IDs remain correct under concurrent delivery.
Failed message persistence does not result in a falsely confirmed durable message.
Valid messages survive actual storage reinitialization.
Messages from unauthorized or disabled accounts are rejected even when the socket remains open.
IRC, REST and event clients receive the same canonical message identity and state.
Alice can send a DM to Bob when allowed.
Bob can read the Alice/Bob conversation.
Alice can read the Alice/Bob conversation.
Charlie cannot read Alice/Bob history.
Charlie cannot retrieve an Alice/Bob message by ID.
Charlie cannot modify an Alice/Bob message.
Charlie cannot delete an Alice/Bob message.
Charlie cannot subscribe to Alice/Bob events.
Charlie cannot retrieve Alice/Bob unread counts.
Charlie cannot enumerate Alice/Bob private attachments.
Alice cannot retrieve Bob/Charlie history.
Alice cannot substitute Bob's account ID to access Bob/Charlie history.
Conversation IDs cannot be manipulated to gain unauthorized access.
DM permissions are checked against the authenticated account, not supplied usernames.
A revoked session loses DM access.
Offline DM persistence preserves the correct recipient identity.
DM history survives restart and remains access-controlled afterward.
DM notifications go only to intended recipients.
DM API and IRC PRIVMSG paths apply consistent access policies.
No DM content appears in ordinary public-channel event streams.
Network administrators do not automatically gain private conversation access unless an explicit, documented administrative policy grants it.
No legacy API endpoint bypasses DM participant checks.
Group-DM membership changes revoke future access according to a clearly defined history policy, if group DMs are supported.
Server-side search cannot reveal other users' DMs.
Protected API without credentials is rejected.
Invalid credentials are rejected.
Expired credentials are rejected.
Revoked credentials are rejected.
Ordinary users cannot invoke admin endpoints.
Changing the HTTP method cannot bypass authorization.
Legacy route aliases enforce the same authorization as `/api/v1`.
Username path parameters cannot impersonate another account.
Channel path parameters cannot bypass membership checks.
Query parameters cannot override authenticated identity.
Request-body IDs cannot override authenticated identity.
Privileged fields cannot be modified through mass assignment.
Invalid input is rejected by runtime validation.
Error responses do not leak database internals, credentials or stack traces.
Unauthorized pagination cannot enumerate protected records.
Bulk operations enforce authorization for every target resource.
OpenAPI-described security requirements match actual route behavior.
Undocumented routes do not accidentally bypass authentication.
Cookie-based mutations enforce CSRF protection.
Cross-origin requests follow the configured CORS policy.
Admin credentials are not accepted through URL query strings.
API responses exclude password hashes, secret keys and private internal attributes.
Restricted responses have appropriate cache-control headers.
Public documentation/health endpoints expose no operational secrets.
Unauthenticated event subscriptions are rejected.
Valid short-lived tickets establish authorized sessions.
Expired tickets are rejected.
Already-consumed tickets are rejected.
Concurrent attempts cannot redeem the same ticket twice.
Tickets for one endpoint cannot authenticate another endpoint.
Tickets cannot be redeemed as another account.
Reusable account credentials are not stored in WebSocket attachments.
Alice receives public events she is authorized to observe.
Alice cannot subscribe to `#staff` without permission.
Charlie cannot subscribe to Alice/Bob DM events.
Revoking channel access prevents future event delivery.
Disabling an account invalidates active event streams.
Session revocation continues to work after Durable Object hibernation.
Reconstructed attachments do not restore stale administrator privileges.
Reconnection cannot bypass authentication.
Event replay does not expose data outside the current access policy.
Event cursors cannot be used to retrieve another user's private events.
Cross-shard delivery respects channel subscription authorization.
Disconnects clean up subscription state.
Slow clients cannot exhaust unbounded buffers.
Duplicate event delivery does not result in unauthorized duplicate mutations.
WebSocket Origin checks and authentication policy are enforced.
Permission changes while the socket is idle take effect without requiring a user to reconnect voluntarily.
Unauthenticated users cannot use privileged service commands.
Users cannot authenticate as another account with invalid credentials.
Users cannot register another user's nickname.
Channel registration requires the defined permissions and prerequisites.
Ordinary members cannot request founder privileges from F.
F OP respects channel access lists.
F DEOP respects hierarchy restrictions.
F VOICE and DEVOICE respect assigned privileges.
F CHANLEV cannot assign permissions exceeding the actor's authority.
F cannot be used to bypass REST authorization.
REST cannot be used to bypass service-bot authorization.
ChanServ access assignments persist across reconnects.
Removing ChanServ access revokes effective privileges.
Unregistered channels do not receive unauthorized service-bot privileges.
Service-bot identities cannot be spoofed by ordinary IRC clients.
Service actions produce the correct audit events.
A user with privileges in one channel cannot use them in another.
Authenticated users can upload within configured limits.
Unauthenticated users cannot upload.
Users cannot delete attachments owned by others without permission.
Private channel attachments are inaccessible to unauthorized users.
DM attachments are inaccessible to nonparticipants.
Guessing media IDs does not bypass authorization.
Signed access links, where used, expire correctly.
Private media is not inadvertently served from public immutable caches.
File-size limits are enforced.
Malicious filenames are safely handled.
Dangerous content types cannot execute as trusted application content.
Users cannot bypass storage quotas.
Deleting an attachment updates persistent metadata correctly.
Expired or removed resources cannot be retrieved through legacy URLs.
Unauthorized users cannot enumerate private upload metadata.
Users can register their own push subscriptions.
Users cannot register subscriptions under another account.
Users cannot list another user's private push endpoints.
Users cannot delete another user's subscriptions.
Disabled accounts cannot use old subscriptions to regain access.
Revoked subscriptions stop receiving notifications.
Private notifications are delivered only to intended accounts.
No private message bodies leak into unrelated notifications.
Notification preferences are enforced.
Invalid or expired push subscriptions are handled safely.
Repeated delivery failures do not cause unbounded retries.
WebPush credentials and subscription secrets do not appear in logs or public APIs.
Account creation writes complete, valid database records.
Account login reads the correct persisted credentials.
Account updates survive runtime restart.
Account disable state survives runtime restart.
Channel registration persists.
Channel metadata updates persist.
Role assignments persist.
Removing roles updates related records correctly.
Message history persists.
Message edits persist.
Redactions persist and do not restore removed content unexpectedly.
Read markers persist.
Foreign-key constraints actually reject invalid references within one database.
Unique constraints reject duplicate records.
Transactions roll back incomplete modifications where appropriate.
Cross-Durable-Object failures do not produce unauthorized permanent state.
Concurrent changes preserve required invariants.
Ninety-day retention removes expired messages.
Retention cleanup does not remove unexpired messages.
Old database migrations preserve existing data.
Deleted accounts do not accidentally cascade-delete unrelated channel history.
Drizzle models match the actual deployed SQLite schema.
Repeated migrations are safe and idempotent where required.
Retry after a successful commit does not create duplicate messages or permissions.
A denied operation leaves stored data unchanged.
A new Durable Object instance cannot assume an unrelated object's database identity.
Query pagination cannot escape the intended account/channel scope.
SQL indexes support bounded history and authorization queries without full-table scans under representative load.
Oversized IRC messages are rejected or handled according to protocol rules.
Oversized WebSocket frames cannot exhaust memory.
Oversized HTTP bodies are rejected.
Authentication requests are rate-limited.
Channel JOIN/PART flooding is controlled.
Channel creation flooding is controlled.
Excessive media uploads are controlled.
History query limits cannot be bypassed using negative or extreme parameters.
Invalid Unicode and malformed IRC tags cannot crash the server.
User-controlled metadata cannot inject unauthorized server message tags.
Excessive event subscriptions cannot exhaust memory.
Slow consumers are disconnected or throttled safely.
Repeated failing RPCs cannot trigger unbounded retry loops.
Malformed API payloads cannot bypass Zod validation.
Concurrent nickname claims result in only one authorized owner.
Concurrent ticket redemption has only one winner.
